content.summary_of_the_paper: This work aims to achieve adversarial robustness within larger bounds against perturbations that may be perceptible, but do not change Oracle prediction. The authors propose a novel defense, Oracle-Aligned Adversarial Training, to align the predictions of the network with that of an Oracle during adversarial training. The method incorporates separate training losses for Oracle-Invariant and Oracle-Sensitive samples in alternate training iterations. In particular, Oracle-Sensitive samples are generated by maximizing Cross-Entropy loss in a PGD attack formulation. In the alternate iteration, the authors use the LPIPS metric to efficiently generate strong Oracle-Invariant attacks during training. Experiments show the improved performance over strong baseline. The paper also shows that High-contrast images are Oracle-Invariant even at large perturbation bounds, whereas Low-Contrast images are Oracle-Sensitive at lower perturbation bounds.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
The paper proposes to and tries to study unrestricted adversarial example, which is good.

Weaknesses:
1. I agree with the authors that "While low-magnitude l_p norm based threat models form a crucial subset of the widely accepted definition of adversarial attacks (Goodfellow & Papernot), they are not sufficient, as there exist valid attacks at higher perturbation bounds as well." That is to say, designing unrestricted adversarial example and its corresponding defense is an important research question. However, the paper fails to study general unrestricted adversarial example, but instead still falls into the category of l_p norm based threat model (though with larger perturbation radius). To me, this is a less interesting problem to study. After all, Oracle-Invariant and Oracle-Sensitive sets are rather subjective objects to be defined for different images and datasets, and I do not think l_p norm can characterize them well.
2. There seems little convincing justification or theory to show why the proposed method works. The novelty of the paper is limited.
3. The experimental improvement is marginal compared with the baselines, with at most 2-3% improvement. Given there might be stronger attack than autoattack, the true improvement can be even smaller or just zero.
4. Different images should use different radiuses to define Oracle-invariant and Oracle-sensitive. The paper uses a constact radius across different images in the training and evaluation phases, which seems inappropriate.
content.summary_of_the_review: Though good experimental performance, the paper lacks convincing justification why the proposed method is better. The improvement in the experimental result is marginal. Given the arms race between empirical defender and attacker, it is hard to believe that the method brings true improvement.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Response to Reviewer UNf3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback. We address some of the common concerns in the general comments section and also post our leaderboard results. We address the specific concerns below:

**Goal of the paper**

While the ultimate goal of adversarial defenses is to achieve robustness aligned with human perception, existing algorithms are far from achieving the same. In fact, even a formal definition of robustness to all perceptual attacks is far fetched at present. Even the paper [1] does not achieve robustness to all attacks within perceptual limits (9.8\% against LPA attack), and relies on $\ell_p$ norm based attacks for evaluations. Against the $\ell_\infty$ norm bound attack of magnitude 8/255, they obtain an accuracy of $28.7\%$ which is significantly lower than the existing $\ell_\infty$ defenses. 

In order to incorporate well-defined metrics for evaluation, $\ell_p$ norm bounds are crucial. While our goals are similarly constrained within this framework, we explore the scalability of existing algorithms to larger perturbation bounds and propose a novel algorithm Oracle Aligned Adversarial Training (OA-AT) to achieve the same. The goal of achieving robustness at larger perturbation bounds requires the consideration of perceptual alignment, since some attacks within this bound can also flip human (or Oracle) prediction. We propose different training losses for oracle invariant and oracle sensitive examples to achieve robustness at large perturbations bounds without compromising on the clean accuracy. We utilize well defined metrics for the evaluation and benchmarking of the proposed defense. As shown in the general comments section, we acheive improvements in robustness against other $\ell_p$ norm bounds and common corruptions as well. 

**Novelty of the method**:

Our goal is to achieve robustness to Oracle Invariant examples within large perturbation bounds without compromising on the clean accuracy. As shown in Table-1, previous works cannot scale to large perturbation bounds due to the conflict in the training objective. Although PGD-AT achieves 32.25% robustness at large perturbation bounds, it is accompanied with a 16.19% drop in clean accuracy. We therefore propose to treat Oracle Invariant and Oracle Sensitive examples separately and design specific losses to achieve robustness at large perturbation bounds without compromising on the clean accuracy. 

Secondly, we explore the connection between image contrast and Oracle sensitivity of adversarial examples for two reasons - firstly, we note that high contrast images produce Oracle Invariant examples and low contrast images produce Oracle sensitive examples (Ref. Fig.4, Fig.15-20). This allows for better evaluation against white-box attacks, since higher contrast images are expected to be more robust to all attacks within a given perturbation bound (as shown in Fig.5). Secondly, based on the results in Table-2, we note that the problem of robustness at large perturbation bounds stems from the fact that contrast levels of images in the training dataset vary largely. Hence, standard adversarial training causes a conflict in training objective for low contrast images, leading to a large drop in clean and robust accuracy. This can open up future directions of research to achieve robustness at larger perturbation bounds. 

Lastly, contrary to prior work [2] we show that weight averaging and Autoaugment can lead to significant gains in robustness even in the absence of additional training data or synthetic data, which can lead to improvements in robustness at standard perturbation bounds as well. 




[1] Cassidy Laidlaw, Sahil Singla, and Soheil Feizi. Perceptual adversarial robustness: Defense against unseen threat models. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2021.

[2] Rebuffi et al., Fixing Data Augmentation to Improve Adversarial Robustness

**Empirical contribution**

We achieve higher gains with large model capacities and long training schedules (200 epochs). As shown below, without the use of additional/ synthetic data, we achieve a significant gain over existing methods on the RobustBench leaderboard. 

In Table-7 of the Appendix, we additionally evaluate against many other attacks and find AutoAttack to be the strongest. Even after evaluating against an ensemble of AutoAttack (AA) and MultiTargeted (MT) attacks [3], our gains are significant either in terms of robust accuracy, or clean accuracy, or both. We note that using MultiTargeted (MT) attack along with AutoAttack (AA) leads to a decrease of only 0.01% in robust accuracy, suggesting that AutoAttack (AA) itself is sufficient for benchmarking robustness. For evaluating robustness at larger perturbation bounds we use an ensemble of strong gradient-free search-based attacks Square and RayS which give Oracle-Invariant images as shown in Fig.6,7 and the "Human evaluation" folder in the supplementary material.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to develop a defense algorithm beyond perceptual limits, which is defined with a small epsilon ball. To this end, the author proposes Oracle-aligned adversarial training that defines the label of generated adversaries with a new scheme (claim as an Oracle), e.g., it utilizes LPIPS representation as approximated Oracle. The author provides extensive experiments on several robustness benchmarks and shows strong empirical robustness.
content.main_review:
**Strength**\
The perspective of this paper is interesting and will give a new insight to the readers.\
The paper provides extensive experiments on several robustness benchmarks.

**Weakness**\
The overall scheme is ill-defined. Due to the unclear definition of “Oracle,” the proposed method is hard to believe the proposed scheme is the best choice.
* I understand the purpose of the author, but the author should rigorously define the “Oracle.”
* Hard to understand the purpose of an Oracle-Invariant attack, i.e., LPIPS. As the adversarial feature is well-transferable across architectures [1], the defined attack will reduce the robust feature of the attack. Due to this reason, it seems like the LPIPS do not affect adversarial robustness much (in Table 4).

The comparison is unfair, as the method strongly utilizes the strong empirical benefit of {weight averaging, augmentations, scheduling}.
* Especially, augmentations [2] and weight averaging [3] are known to be beneficial to improve robustness.
* Also, the scheme needs careful engineering, such as scheduling. 
* For a fair comparison, removing the arguments is needed rather than adding them into AWP [4].

Although the paper aims to achieve robustness beyond the perceptual limit, it still considers the careful design of small epsilon ball constraints. If the author defines a training scheme w.o any epsilon ball constraint, it will be more convincing.

Additional adversarial training is required for the model in LPIPS regularization.
* While the motivation is to define Oracle prediction (to achieve beyond perceptual limits), this network needs careful design of epsilon ball size.

The experimental results slightly differ from the original paper’s results [4]. 
* Comparing the result with the reported value of [4], it is hard to claim the proposed scheme is state-of-the-art.
* Considering an additional experimental setup will strengthen the paper, i.e., running 200 epochs (the author only considered it in CIFAR-100).

Additionally, I realize that in that main text, the authors are referring to some important analysis in the appendix, e.g., Fig 8 and ablation study. If the analysis is important in understanding the paper, please move the section into the main text.

**Questions**\
Can the author provide the computation time, i.e., training time? I believe adversarial training requires much more time [5] than standard training, and the proposed scheme might suffer from such constraints. 

**References**\
[1] Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features, Ilyas et al., NeurIPS 2019\
[2] Relating Adversarially Robust Generalization to Flat Minima, Stutz et al., ICCV 2021\
[3] Robust Overfitting may be mitigated by properly learned smoothening, Chen et al., ICLR 2021\
[4] Adversarial Weight Perturbation Helps Robust Generalization, Wu et al., NeurIPS 2020\
[5] Fast is better than free: Revisiting adversarial training, Wong et al., ICLR 2020
content.summary_of_the_review:
I recommend weak rejection.\
I agree that the perspective of this paper is interesting. However, the overall scheme is ill-defined, and hard to agree on the claim due to the weaknesses. I believe another round of revision is needed for better clarification and believe it will largely strengthen the paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AS8k
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their valuable feedback. We address some of the common concerns in the general comments section and also post our leaderboard results. We address the specific concerns below:

We refer to human opinion as the Oracle label.  The ideal goal of an adversarial defense is indeed to align with the Oracle. However, as mentioned in Section-3.3, we only consider a subset of these ideal goals - that is, to achieve robustness to imperceptible attacks (such as those within $\varepsilon=8/255$ for CIFAR-10), and to achieve robustness to Oracle Invariant attacks at larger perturbation bounds. We do not directly consider the goal of exactly matching the prediction of the model with that of the Oracle for Oracle-sensitive samples, since training and evaluation using Oracle labels is challenging. However, we allow Oracle-sensitive samples to align with both the original and target class (using mixup-based loss) to prevent a large drop in clean accuracy. We thus incorporate the goal of achieving a better robustness-accuracy tradeoff as well. 

**LPIPS based attack**: As rightly pointed by the reviewer, the LPIPS regularizer indeed generates Oracle Invariant attacks by reducing robust features in the attack. While this does weaken the attack, as shown in Fig.10, the right choice of the weight of the LPIPS regularizer can generate attacks that are both Oracle Invariant and also sufficiently strong to fool the model. This is better for training when compared to stronger PGD attacks as they do not lead to a conflict in the training objective as shown in Fig.2 while also inducing robustness in the model. As shown in Table-4 (E2), without the LPIPS regularizer there is 1.8% drop in clean accuracy and also a drop in robust accuracy. The effect is more pronounced in WideResNet models as shown below:


|               | **Clean**| **GAMA (8/255)** | **Square (16/255)** |
|---------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|
|               |  **CIFAR-10, WRN-34-10** |            |               |
| Ours          |                85.32 |      58.48 |         36.93 |
| Ours (without lpips) |                83.47 |      57.58 |         36.68 |
| AWP           |                85.36 |      56.34 |          31.7 |
|               | **CIFAR-100, WRN-34-10** |            |               |
| Ours          |                65.73 |       30.90 |         18.47 |
| Ours (without lpips) |                63.16 |      30.22 |         18.42 |
| AWP           |                62.73 |      29.92 |         15.85 |

**Comparision of our approach without autoaugment and weight averaging**

We would like to highlight that we do not use autoaugment and weight averaging with our approach for CIFAR-10 on ResNet-18. Therefore, these results in Table-3(a) show the clear benefit of the proposed approach over prior methods. 
We observe gains with AutoAugment on datasets with larger number of classes such as CIFAR-100 on large capacity models such as WideResNet as it helps in preventing overfitting, specifically while training at large perturbation bounds. We show results of CIFAR-100 on WRN-34-10 without the use of AutoAugment and Weight Averageing below: 


| Method  | Clean Accuracy | GAMA (8/255) | Square (16/255) |
|----------------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------|:--------------------:|
| AWP   |           62.78 |        29.82 |            15.7 |
| AWP+ (With AutoAugment)           |          61.33 |        29.22 |           15.18 |
| AWP+ (With Weight Averaging)    |          62.73 |        29.92 |           15.85 |
| AWP+ (With AutoAugment and Weight Averaging)       |          62.23 |        29.36 |           15.47 |
| Ours    |      65.73     |     30.90     |      18.47      |
| Ours (Without Weight Averaging)       |      65.53     |     30.59    |      18.06      |
| Ours (Without AutoAugment)           |      66.23     |     30.27    |      18.35      |

We note that even without Weight Averaging and AutoAugment, we achieve significant gains over the AWP baseline. 

We would like to highlight that the scheduling of $\varepsilon$, $\alpha$ and $\lambda$ are common across all datasets, and are not hyperparameters to be tuned. The scheduling of $\varepsilon$ has also been done in prior work [3]. 
The value of $\varepsilon$ at which robustness is desired is a specification and not a training parameter. The proposed approach works best for a medium $\varepsilon$ bound where the perception of the adversarial examples change marginally. 

[1] Relating Adversarially Robust Generalization to Flat Minima, Stutz et al., ICCV 2021

[2] Cassidy Laidlaw, Sahil Singla, and Soheil Feizi. Perceptual adversarial robustness: Defense against unseen threat models. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2021.

[3] Amirreza Shaeiri, Rozhin Nobahari, and Mohammad Hossein Rohban. Towards deep learning models resistant to large perturbations. arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.13370, 2020.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies adversarially robust learning in the setting where relatively large perturbations are allowed, i.e., the perturbations are large enough that they can change the true label of an image according to an oracle (say, a human). The authors claim that learning in such a setting boils down to ensuring that the model is invariant to perturbations that do not change the oracle's prediction (Oracle-Invariant; OI) yet is sensitive to perturbations that do (Oracle-Sensitive; OS). They then propose a training scheme based on this intuition. Concretely, they train the model on two types of examples: (a) standard white-box adversarial examples but with a soft label that corresponds to a convex combinations of the models prediction on the original and perturbed example, (b) OI adversarial examples which are constructed by regularizing the LPIPS metric between the original and perturbed sample. Evaluating their method, the authors find that it offers a small improvement over existing methods on standard benchmarks. Finally, the authors draw a connection between the contrast of an image and its intrinsic robustness according to an oracle.
content.main_review:
The paper studies an important problem: how can we approach robustness to perturbations that are not guaranteed to be imperceptible. However, the paper lacks focus and rigor at a number of places:

- Sections 3.3: From what I understand, the robustness goal can be stated simply as "the model should agree with the oracle". Why is the distinction between OI and OS examples important at this point?
- The major challenge here is obtaining access to an oracle the we can incorporate into training. The authors consider a very crude approximation based on the LPIPS metric. However, there is no rigorous evaluation of how well this metric performs or whether the examples produced are actually invariant for a human. Additionally, this approximation of an oracle by the LPIPS metric is first mentioned in page 6, which feels misleading given how central this approximation is to the work.
- The title is somewhat misleading. "Beyond perceptual limits" implies that the model is more robust that what humans can perceive.
- The connections to image contrast is interesting yet tangential and specific to the specific benchmarks used. If the goal of the paper is to propose a general methodology for incorporating an oracle into training then image contrast seems overly specific (it is not a general methodology for estimating per-image epsilon values).
- Based on the abstract and introduction, the goal of the paper is to develop methods for training and evaluating models in a setting where robustness is defined with respect to an oracle. However, the treatment of the topic ends up being too narrow, and boils down to training with LPIPS-regularized adversarial examples and PGD-examples with soft labels. It is thus not clear why this is a significant departure from previous work.
- There is no rigorous study of whether the OI examples created for evaluation are actually OI. For all we know, they might be actually flipping the oracle label and the fact that the model is robust could hint towards the existence of invariance-based adversarial examples.
- The description of the methodology could be improved. For instance, in page 6, experimental details (exact eps thresholds) are interspersed into the description of the general algorithm thus masking the key intuition.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, while the premise of the study is interesting, the manuscript lacks the clarity, rigor, and focus that is required to make a significant contribution.

While the Oracle-Invariance of the Square attack is satisfied by design, we additionally show images in Fig.6 of the Appendix and in the folder "Human evaluation" in the Supplementary material. We additionally plan to include a formal human annotation of these images in the final version. 

- We will improve the description of the methodology to exclude the exact epsilon values. 

We will be happy to answer any further concerns as well.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors proposed adversarial training for moderate size perturbation (e.g. $8 \leq \epsilon \leq 16$ on CIFAR-10). The main idea is to use standard PGD attack for Oracle Sensitive Adversarial examples and regularized PGD with LPIPS distance for Oracle Invariant Adversarial examples. In the experiments, the proposed method, so-called Oracle-Aligned Adversarial Training, improves robustness for standard thresholds (e.g. $\epsilon = 8$ for CIFAR-10) and moderately large thresholds (e.g. $\epsilon = 16$ for CIFAR-10).
content.main_review:
### Strengths:
- Novel definition of Oracle-Sensitive and Oracle-Invariant attacks.
- Hypothesise and show that high contrast images are Oracle-Invariant at large perturbation.
- Relative improvement of 10-15% for small attacks and medium strength attacks in experiments on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets.
- Exemplary and comprehensive experimental comparison of adversarial robustness according to the research standards.

### Weaknesses:
- The authors claim to explore the $l_p$-norm robustness beyond perceptual limits. To strengthen their claims, the authors can include experiments with human annotators to show that the predictions of the model are indeed perceptually aligned, as it was done in [1, 2] on experiments with human annotators.
- The method combines many different techniques and has many different hyperparameters ($\alpha$, $\lambda$, probability of AutoAugment, schedule for $\epsilon$, $\alpha$, $\lambda$, early stopping). The final accuracy and robustness are highly sensitive to these various hyperparameters.
- Given the various hyperparameters, it is not clear how to scale the proposed defence to ImageNet as it will require fine-tuning each hyperparameter. Maybe authors can comment about the stability of the method to the final hyperparameter choice and overall budget for the hyperparameter search used in experiments.

### Questions / comments:
- $l_{\infty}$-AT models usually are non-robust to other $l_p$-norm perturbations. Can the authors include experiments for other attack norms?

[1] Matyasko, A., & Chau, Lap-Pui, Improved network robustness with adversary critic, In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (2018).

[2] Laidlaw, C., Singla, S., & Feizi, S., Perceptual adversarial robustness: defense against unseen threat models, In  International Conference on Learning Representations (2021).
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper introduces several novel ideas. The authors conduct a comprehensive and exemplary evaluation of the proposed defense to show its effectiveness. The language and presentation are also quite clear.

Overall, I recommend accepting this paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5p75
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their encouraging comments and suggestions. 

**Correlation of model prediction with Human annotators**

We include High Contrast (HC), Low Contrast (LC), and Medium Contrast (HC) images along with the corresponding adversarial examples generated using PGD 10 step attack with the LPIPS regularizer, Square attack with 5000 queries, GAMA PGD-100 attack at $\varepsilon=16/255$ for CIFAR-10 dataset in the folder "Human evaluation" in the Supplementary material. We include corresponding images for the SVHN dataset as well, for $\varepsilon=12/255$. Based on an informal human annotation on these images, we present the following observations:
- Standard white-box attacks generate Oracle-Sensitive examples for low contrast images and Oracle-Invariant examples for high contrast images
- Using the LPIPS regularizer in a PGD attack produces Oracle Invariant images 
- Square attack produces Oracle Invariant images

We will do a more formal human annotation adhering to the accepted guidelines and present the same in the final version. 

Based on this, we note that our evaluation criteria at large epsilon bounds are indeed designed to ensure that the model prediction aligns with human perception as follows:
- Accuracy against Square and Ray-S Attack (Table-3, Main paper)
- Accuracy against LPIPS regularized attack (Fig.9, Appendix)
- GAMA attack accuracy on High Contrast images (Fig.5, Main paper)

**Sensitivity to Hyperparameters**

While the proposed approach introduces two additional hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\lambda$, we show in Fig. 12 and 13 of the Appendix that the results are stable across variations in these values. An initial guess for $\lambda$ can be obtained by observing a few attacked images as shown in Fig.10 of the Appendix. In fact, **the same hyperparameters that are found on the CIFAR-10 dataset can be used on CIFAR-100 and SVHN as well** as shown in the below table. The probability of AutoAugment has also been set to 1 and not tuned specifically. Finetuning specifically for each dataset merely results in a marginal boost as shown below:

|                                     |         Clean        | GAMA (4/255) | Square (12/255) | GAMA (8/255) |
|-------------------------------------|:--------------------:|:------------:|:---------------:|:------------:|
|                                     | |        **SVHN, PreActResNet18**       |                 |              |
|                 AWP                 |         91.91        |     75.92    |      35.78      |     53.88    |
|                 Ours                |         94.61        |     78.37    |      39.56      |     55.15    |
| Ours (CIFAR-10 hyperparameters) |         95.17        |     78.16    |      39.12      |     54.77    |

|                                     |        Clean        | GAMA (8/255) | Square (16/255) |
|-------------------------------------|:-------------------:|:------------:|:---------------:|
|                                     | **CIFAR100, WRN-34-10** |              |                 |
|                 AWP                 |        62.73        |     29.92    |      15.85      |
|                 Ours                |        65.73        |     30.9     |      18.47      |
| Ours (CIFAR-10 hyperparameters) |        64.66        |     31.18    |      17.93      |

We do not use early stopping for our approach and use it only to obtain competent results for the baselines. 
Lastly, for tuning the hyperparameters $\alpha$ and $\lambda$, we merely need to run the last one-fourth of the training, and not the full run, as these parameters are used only at large perturbation bounds. The schedule for $\alpha$, $\lambda$, and $\varepsilon$ are fixed and do not change across different runs, hence they are not hyperparameters that need to be tuned. 

**Results against other $\ell_p$ norm bound perturbations**

We request the reviewer to kindly refer to the table in the general comments (Comparison with RobustBench Leaderboard results) section above for the results. We obtain a significant boost over the baseline method against other $\ell_p$ norm bound attacks and common corruptions as well.

content.title: A note to all reviewers
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewers for their time and valuable feedback on our work. We are happy to see that some of the reviewers find our work novel and significant, our evaluations comprehensive and thorough, and our results noteworthy. We will certainly work towards incorporating all the suggestions in our updated version.


We first address a few common concerns, and will further address the individual concerns of each of the reviewers in the next few days.

**Goal of the paper**

While the ultimate goal of adversarial defenses is to achieve robustness aligned with human perception, existing algorithms are far from achieving the same. In fact, even a formal definition of robustness to all perceptual attacks is far fetched at present. Even the paper [1] does not achieve robustness to all attacks within perceptual limits (9.8\% against LPA attack), and relies on $\ell_p$ norm based attacks for evaluations. Against the $\ell_\infty$ norm bound attack of magnitude 8/255, they obtain an accuracy of $28.7\%$ which is significantly lower than the existing $\ell_\infty$ defenses. 

In order to incorporate well-defined metrics for evaluation, $\ell_p$ norm bounds are crucial. While our goals are similarly constrained within this framework, we explore the scalability of existing algorithms to larger perturbation bounds and propose a novel algorithm Oracle Aligned Adversarial Training (OA-AT) to achieve the same. The goal of achieving robustness at larger perturbation bounds requires the consideration of perceptual alignment, since some attacks within this bound can also flip human (or Oracle) prediction. We propose different training losses for oracle invariant and oracle sensitive examples to achieve robustness at large perturbations bounds without compromising on the clean accuracy. While we use LPIPS metric to generate Oracle-Invariant images for training, we utilize well defined metrics for the evaluation and benchmarking of the proposed defense. 

[1] Cassidy Laidlaw, Sahil Singla, and Soheil Feizi. Perceptual adversarial robustness: Defense against unseen threat models. International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2021.

**Use of LPIPS based regularizer for training**

As shown in Fig.10 of the Appendix, the LPIPS regularizer indeed ensures perceptual similarity between clean and perturbed images by disrupting the spatial correlation of the perturbations. This is also justified in [1] based on human annotation. Fig.8 in the Appendix shows that LPIPS computed from an adversarially trained model can identify Oracle-Invariant samples. 

As shown in the below table, without the LPIPS regularizer, there is a significant drop in the clean accuracy. 


|               | **Clean**                | **GAMA (8/255)** | **Square (16/255)** |
|---------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|
|               |  **CIFAR-10, WRN-34-10** |            |               |
| Ours          |                85.32 |      58.48 |         36.93 |
| Ours (without lpips) |                83.47 |      57.58 |         36.68 |
| AWP           |                85.36 |      56.34 |          31.7 |
|               | **CIFAR-100, WRN-34-10** |            |               |
| Ours          |                65.73 |       30.9 |         18.47 |
| Ours (without lpips) |                63.16 |      30.22 |         18.42 |
| AWP           |                62.73 |      29.92 |         15.85 |

content.title: Comparison with RobustBench Leaderboard results
content.comment:
We agree with reviewer *AS8k* that it is important to compare our results with the official numbers reported by AWP at a similar computational budget. We report results with 200 epochs of training for CIFAR-10 and 110 epochs of training for CIFAR-100 below. Our results are currently state-of-the-art amongst the methods that do not use additional/synthetic data on the RobustBench [2] leaderboard. Despite obtaining 4.44% improvement in robust accuracy against Oracle Invariant attacks at 16/255, we also obtain 1.87% accuracy on **AutoAttack (AA)** accuracy at 8/255 as well. We obtain similarly large gains on CIFAR-100 as well, against our implementation of the AWP defense which is better than the results on the leaderboard. The gains obtained are significantly larger than the previous methods on the leaderboard without additional data.

We obtain significant gains against other $\ell_p$ norm bound attacks such as $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$ and $\ell_0$ as well when compared to the baseline. We obtain improvements against common corruptions as well, which is also better compared to models of larger capacity on the RobustBench leaderboard.

**We request the reviewers to kindly reconsider our contributions and share their feedback, which will help us respond better during this rebuttal period.**
